units.title: Likelihood and perplexity, and their limits
outcomes: Derive token-weighted perplexity with an explicit valid-token mask and state the conditional form for prompt-conditioned scoring.
Explain why perplexity comparisons need the same tokenizer, data split and conditioning before any ranking claim.
Read word, byte and bits-per-byte variants from an evaluation config and say which one removes tokenizer effects.
units.why: Perplexity guides training and scaling because it is smooth, but it scores every token including ones the task does not care about. A lower number on different tokenizers or splits is not a better model.

next.note: Carry perplexity limits into explicit task contracts and metric choices.
Treat perplexity gaps with slices and intervals instead of reading them as wins.

focus: The mean runs over scored tokens only. Prompt tokens leave both the sum and the count in the conditional form.
Perplexity is \(\exp\) of the mean negative log likelihood, so it reads as the effective shortlist size at each step.
A new tokenizer changes the token count for the same text, so the means run over different units. Bits per byte divides by bytes to remove that effect.
Perplexity is smooth and universal for scaling, but it penalizes tokens the task ignores. Task accuracy still needs its own contract.
units.reproduce: From correct-token probs 0.5, 0.7 and 0.5, derive the mean negative log likelihood 0.58 and the perplexity 1.79 by hand, then state the conditional form for a prompt plus response.
traps: Comparing perplexity across tokenizers or splits. Different vocabularies split the same text into different token counts, so the ranking is meaningless.
Reading a low perplexity as chat quality, reasoning or safety. The lecture and notebook both limit it to language modeling and pretraining monitoring.
Trusting submitted perplexity numbers without checking that probs sum to one. Accuracy needs only output text, but perplexity needs valid probabilities.

selfTest.a: About 1.79. The mean negative log likelihood is \(-(\ln 0.5 + \ln 0.7 + \ln 0.5)/3 = 0.58\), and \(\exp(0.58) = 1.79\).
selfTest.q: Correct-token probs are 0.5, 0.7 and 0.5. What is the perplexity?

selfTest.a: The first, if both scored the same text. Per-token means use different denominators, so compare totals instead: \(2.0 \times 100 = 200\) nats versus \(1.8 \times 150 = 270\) nats. The first model gives the text higher probability even though its per-token perplexity looks worse; bits per byte makes the same comparison.
selfTest.q: Two tokenizers score the same text with mean NLL 2.0 over 100 tokens and 1.8 over 150 tokens. Which model is better?

selfTest.a: Perplexity computes from the model's own probabilities, so they must sum to one. A task accuracy check only reads generated text and does not need that trust.
selfTest.q: Why does the lecture warn that a perplexity leaderboard must trust the model?

selfTest.a: When a prompt is given and only the response matters. Score \(p(\text{response} \mid \text{prompt})\) normalized by response length, so prompt tokens do not dilute the number.
selfTest.q: When should you report conditional perplexity instead of full perplexity?

Implement exact and normalized match plus a structured verifier, and show a counterexample for each automatic metric.
Retain raw outputs and version the task, prompt, parsing and model so another run reproduces the score.
units.why: Most evaluation gains come from parsing, prompts or versions, not from the model. A contract plus raw outputs turns a score into evidence that survives review.

next.note: Route open-ended outputs from this harness into judged evaluation with bias controls.

focus: The task is the prompt plus few-shot plus parsing plus version, not just the dataset name. Change any part and the score means something new.
Strict match needs the #### marker, flexible extract takes the last number. The same outputs can pass one and fail the other.
acc picks the highest-prob choice, acc_norm corrects for length. IFEval strict_acc checks format and keywords, not whether the answer is right.
Keep raw generations and the config hash. Reruns compare filtered outputs, not just the mean.
units.reproduce: From one GSM8K output without a #### marker that states the right number, show strict-match failing while flexible-extract passes, then write the version string that would catch the parser change.
traps: Comparing scores across papers with different prompts, few-shot counts or parsers. The notebook calls such comparisons invalid without aligned configs.
Treating flexible-extract as strict. Lenient parsing inflates the score without changing the model.
Reading IFEval strict accuracy as semantic quality. It verifies constraints such as word count and keywords, not the meaning of the response.

selfTest.a: Strict fails because there is no #### (number) match, while flexible extracts the last number-like token 42 and passes. Report both pipeline names with the score.
selfTest.q: An output says The answer is 42 with no #### marker. How do strict-match and flexible-extract score it?

selfTest.a: acc compares raw choice loglikelihoods, acc_norm normalizes by length or bytes. Use the normalized form when choices differ in length or tokenization, and state which one the table uses.
selfTest.q: When should you report acc_norm instead of acc?

selfTest.a: Use temperature 0 with do_sample false for exact and structured metrics. Use non-zero temperature only for pass@k, self-consistency or robustness runs, and then fix the seed.
selfTest.q: Which temperature and sampling settings suit deterministic task metrics?

selfTest.a: Task YAML plus commit hash, prompt text, few-shot count and split, filter regexes, generation kwargs, model version and evaluator version, plus raw outputs saved with log_samples and output_path.
selfTest.q: What must be versioned for a task result to be reproducible?

units.stopWhen: Your harness records prompt, few-shot, parser and versions with raw outputs, and you can show one output where strict and flexible disagree.

units.title: Model judges and human review
outcomes: Explain position, length, style, identity and verbosity biases in model judges and the fix for each.
Explain when human review and adjudication subsets are needed instead of another automatic metric.
Measure judge disagreement with a position-swap study and report residual uncertainty against a human or deterministic subset.
units.why: Open-ended quality has no ground truth, so a judge is a measuring instrument with its own errors. Without bias controls and a human spot check, win rates measure style more than correctness.

next.note: Carry judge error into slices and intervals instead of quoting a bare win rate.
Human adjudication subsets are the same discipline the applied-science investigations require.

focus: Randomize order and average both directions. A judge that flips with position is reporting position, not quality.
Report LC win rate with raw win rate and average length. Longer answers win raw comparisons even when they are worse.
Checklists and rubrics beat single scores for both human and model judges. WildBench uses them for that reason.
One judge model is one instrument. Cross-check with a second judge plus a human or deterministic subset before claiming a win.
units.reproduce: Run the position-swap study on one answer pair three times each way, compute the inconsistency rate, and state the LC win rate with the average lengths.
traps: Treating a single GPT-4 score as ground truth. Agreement with humans depends on task, prompt, version and format.
Assuming length control fixes everything. It corrects length, not position, style, identity or verbosity effects.
Skipping human review because the judge correlates with Arena. Correlation on past prompts does not certify your task.

selfTest.a: Position bias. Randomize the order, average both directions, and report the inconsistency rate before trusting the verdict.
selfTest.q: The judge picks answer A when it is first, then answer B after a swap. What is that, and what fixes it?

selfTest.a: The LC rate. Raw win rate is inflated by length, so check average length and inspect a subset by hand.
selfTest.q: Model X has higher raw win rate but lower LC win rate than baseline, with much longer outputs. Which rate should you trust?

selfTest.a: \(p(A \text{ beats } B) = 1/(1 + 10^{(ELO_B - ELO_A)/400})\). Fit ELO scores to maximize the likelihood of the observed pairwise wins.
selfTest.q: How does Chatbot Arena turn pairwise votes into ELO scores?

selfTest.a: When correctness matters rather than style, when judge disagreement is high, or when the risk is high. Size the subset by risk and budget, judge with a checklist, and keep every raw judgment.
selfTest.q: When is human adjudication required?

units.title: Uncertainty, robustness and honest claims
outcomes: Build slices, paired comparisons and bootstrap intervals for a small evaluation, and read overlapping intervals correctly.
Measure prompt, order and sampling sensitivity under fixed compute budgets and report the range, not just the best run.
Separate capability results from safety results with distinct gates and stop conditions.
units.why: A single mean hides where a model fails and how fragile the number is. Slices plus uncertainty plus sensitivity turn a leaderboard entry into a claim you can defend.

next.note: Add the contamination boundary to the release gate.
Carry interval discipline into quality-compute comparisons with uncertainty ranges.

focus: Slice first, then aggregate. Report per-slice means before any composite, and say which slice drives the headline.
Compare paired deltas on the same prompts, not two independent means. Pairing cancels prompt difficulty, which two independent intervals would both include.
Bootstrap resamples with replacement and reports the std of the stat. Use the closed-form SE for plain means and bootstrap for medians, F1, perplexity and similar.
Fix the sampling and prompt budget before comparing. Temperature, seed, few-shot and prompt version are part of the result.
units.reproduce: From the Exercise 3 scores, compute arithmetic means (A 74.0, B 73.8) and geometric means (A 73.7, B 73.7), then state which model is more balanced and why the headline mean misleads.
traps: Reading overlapping intervals as proof of no difference without a paired test. Pair the prompts first, then test the \(\delta\).
Reporting the best prompt or seed. Prompt swings of 5 to 15 percent dwarf small model gaps.
Claiming safety from a capability average. A model at 90 math and 10 safety averages 50 and is still unsafe, so gate safety separately.

selfTest.a: Arithmetic: A 74.0, B 73.8, so A leads by 0.25. Geometric: both about 73.7, so the gap vanishes. B is more balanced (range 8 versus 17) because the geometric mean punishes the weak 65 that the headline average hides.
selfTest.q: Exercise 3 scores Model A at 82, 71, 65, 78 and Model B at 78, 75, 70, 72. What do the two means say?

selfTest.a: Plain means and acc_all have closed forms (mean_stderr, acc_all_stderr). Medians, F1, perplexity, BLEU and similar use bootstrap_stderr with resampling, and groups combine with pooled_sample_stderr.
selfTest.q: When should you use bootstrap_stderr instead of a closed-form SE?

selfTest.a: Both models see the same prompts, so prompt difficulty cancels and the \(\delta\) isolates the model effect. Independent means mix model differences with prompt sampling noise.
selfTest.q: Why compare paired deltas rather than two independent means?

selfTest.a: Gate them separately with distinct primary tasks, regressions, slices, safety checks and stop conditions. Dual-use tasks such as CyBench count as both, so state which claim each result supports.
selfTest.q: How should capability and safety results be gated?

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: 20-example two-slice evaluator with raw outputs, paired deltas and bootstrap intervals, plus one deliberate prompt or sampling failure.
units.stopWhen: Your two-slice report shows per-slice means, a paired \(\delta\) with an interval, and a sensitivity range for one prompt or sampling change.

focus: Run both exact and approximate (n-gram or embedding) checks. Exact catches copies, n-grams catch near copies.
check_integrity checks task and data plumbing, not training overlap. Do not cite it as decontamination.
Duplicates and memorized benchmarks inflate scores without new capability. Prefer fresh or private evals for the headline claim.
Report full versus clean side by side. A large drop is evidence of leakage, not a worse model.
units.reproduce: Write the 13-gram overlap scan from decontamination.md: build eval n-grams, scan training n-grams, mark contaminated docs, and report the metric with a decontaminate suffix on the clean subset.
traps: Equating deduplication with decontamination. Dedup cleans training, while decontamination checks train versus eval overlap.
Trusting timestamps for freshness. Copied text carries old dates into new pages, so scraped evals still need overlap checks.
Claiming reasoning from a memorized benchmark. Unique tasks or fresh problems test generalization, while leaked sets test recall.

selfTest.a: 13. OpenAI used 8 to 13 by dataset, and the harness fixes 13 for simplicity. A doc is contaminated if any 13-gram overlaps a training doc.
selfTest.q: Which \(n\) does the harness use for decontamination, and what marks a doc as contaminated?

selfTest.a: It checks task and data integrity such as config and loading, not train-eval overlap. It cannot replace decontamination.
selfTest.q: What does check_integrity do, and what does it not do?

selfTest.a: Move to HumanEval+ or LiveCodeBench, run overlap checks, and cross-validate with more sets, because 164 items carry high variance on their own.
selfTest.q: HumanEval is stale and widely memorized. What should you do?

selfTest.a: Report both, headline the clean number, and present the drop as leakage evidence. Never claim broad capability from the full score alone.
selfTest.q: Full-set accuracy is 85 percent but clean-subset accuracy is 71 percent. What should you claim?

study.title: CS336 Assignment 3: IsoFLOPs method and offline curves

focus: Count each projection separately under GQA: \(Q\) stays \(D\) by \(H\) times \(d_h\), while \(K\) and \(V\) shrink to \(D\) by \(K\) times \(d_h\). MHA \(4D^2\) is the special case \(K\) equals \(H\).

One matmul \([m, k]\) by \([k, n]\) costs \(2mkn\). Sum \(Q\), \(K\), \(V\), \(QK^\top\), \(AV\) and \(O\) plus gate, up and down plus unembedding \(2BSDV\), and do not drop the \(V\) term at large \(V\).
Backward costs about twice forward, so training is about 6 times params times tokens for short contexts. Long \(S\) adds the \(2LS\) term.
IsoFLOPs fixes \(C\) and varies \(N\), finds the loss minimum per budget, then fits \(N_{opt}\) and \(D_{opt}\) power laws. Fit the offline points, and do not burn the hosted budget.
units.reproduce: Derive the LLaMA-2 70B count from \(D\)8192 \(L\)80 \(V\)32000 as \(2VD\) plus \(12LD^2\) equals 64.9B, then the 70B 15T training total 6.3e24 FLOPs and the 144-day estimate on 1024 H100s at MFU 0.5.
traps: Counting MACs as FLOPs. One multiply-accumulate is two FLOPs, so double the thop MACS number.
Comparing runs by steps at different batch sizes. Convert to tokens first: batch times steps times length.
Fitting IsoFLOPs on the hosted API when the exercise gives offline curves. The bounded task uses isoflops_curves.json only.

selfTest.a: \(80 \times 10^9 \times 8/12 = 53.3\text{B}\). It is an upper bound because activations are not counted.
selfTest.q: What is the largest AdamW model on 8 H100s at 12 bytes per param?

selfTest.a: \(2 \times 32000 \times 8192 + 12 \times 80 \times 8192^2 = 0.52\text{B} + 64.42\text{B}\), about 64.9B. The real model has about 69B: GQA shrinks \(K\) and \(V\), but its SwiGLU width of 28672 is well above \(8D/3\), which more than makes up for it. The \(12LD^2\) shortcut assumes MHA and a \(4D\)-equivalent FFN.
selfTest.q: What does \(2VD\) plus \(12LD^2\) give for LLaMA-2 70B?

selfTest.a: Forward is \(2NP\) and backward is \(4NP\) (one matmul for \(dW\) plus one for \(dX\) per op), so training is \(6NP\). Raschka measures forward with thop then triples it for forward plus backward.
selfTest.q: Why is the training rule \(6NP\)?

selfTest.a: Group runs by \(C\), take the min-loss \(N\) per budget (or a quadratic fit), fit \(N_{opt}\) and \(D_{opt}\) power laws in \(C\), then extrapolate to the target budget such as 1e23 or 1e24 in exercise units.
selfTest.q: What are the IsoFLOPs fitting steps?

focus: State the precision for every term. Mixed bf16 params and grads with fp32 master and moments is 12 bytes without master and 16 to 18 with it, so measure to confirm which ledger your loop keeps.
Compare arithmetic intensity to accelerator intensity (H100 about 295). Below it you are memory-bound no matter how good the kernels are.
Prefill grows with \(B\) times \(T\) for MLP and \(S/2\) for attention, while generation sits at \(B\) for MLP and below 1 for attention. Batching rescues MLP generation, not attention.
Expect measured memory above the formula. Name allocator caching, fragmentation, graph, workspace and framework overhead before doubting the math.
units.reproduce: Derive the 13B training total from Exercise 2 inputs (fixed 208GB plus BF16 activations 617GB equals 825GB, 11 A100 80GB units) and the H100 \(B\) above 295 compute-bound rule, then reconcile one measured number with named overheads.
traps: Quoting the formula as the fit result. torch.cuda.memory_allocated includes caching and fragmentation, so report both numbers and explain the gap.
Assuming a bigger batch fixes generation attention. Its intensity stays below 1 because each sequence owns its KV, while batching only helps the MLP part.
Comparing quality at unequal compute. Fix prompts, decoding, budgets and evaluator versions, then report quality with compute ranges.
